So, a little music history:
Beethoven titled his Op. 27 No. 2, published in 1802, "Sonata quasi una fantasia," or "Fantasy-ISH Sonata," which is the same title he used for Op. 27 No.1. The moniker "Moonlight" was coined by the poet Ludwig Rellstab, some 22 years later. But by the 1830's "Moonlight" was already the common nickname in Germany and in England.
"Moonlight" really only describes the first movement; the third movement, in particular, may be better nicknamed "Lunar Impact." ("Sonata quasi un'impatto lunare.")

It's a noun that is plural in form but not in meaning, like its synonym "surroundings."  You can talk about your environs or your surroundings, but not one environ or one surrounding.  

MILIEU means the same thing, but is singular in form. Thus, you can make it plural as either "milieux" (the French way) or "milieus" (the regularized way).  But then it means various different settings, which neither of the others can.  "Vicinity/-ies" works the same way as MILIEU/x/s.

The rule of singular clue, singular answer and plural clue, plural answer relates to the meaning of the words, not their grammatical form.

Perhaps usage is different in Australia, but in the US, single letters, especially lower-case ones, are pluralized with an apostrophe to make them more readable. 

Consider these sentences:

I did a crossword that didn’t have any as, is or us.  

I did a crossword that didn’t have any a’s, i’s or u’s. 

Do a little poking around the internet, and you’ll see that most style books, including the prestigious Chicago Manual, support this.
